note.explanation: Hydrocarbons are compounds made only of carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with single bonds between their carbon atoms. Their reactions and physical properties depend on their structure and size.
examples: Methane (CH₄) is the main component of natural gas.
Complete combustion of propane produces carbon dioxide and water.
note.checkAnswer: A mixture of natural gas and air can explode when ignited because the gas burns rapidly in oxygen and releases heat.
note.simple: Hydrocarbons contain carbon and hydrogen only. When they burn completely, they produce carbon dioxide, water and heat.
note.checkQuestion: What are the products of complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
note.title: Hydrocarbons and alkanes
steps: Identify the type of hydrocarbon and its structure.
For combustion, write the hydrocarbon reacting with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water.
Balance the equation by balancing carbon, then hydrogen, then oxygen.
For comparisons, consider molecular size and whether the molecules are straight-chain or branched.
note.answer: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes have carbon–carbon single bonds and undergo combustion, substitution and cracking reactions.

mcqs.stem: Which other atom is almost always present along with carbon atom in all organic compounds?
rationales: Oxygen is present in many organic compounds, but it is not almost always present.
Nitrogen occurs in some organic compounds, but not almost all of them.
Hydrogen is almost always present with carbon in organic compounds.
Halogens occur only in some organic compounds.

mcqs.stem: Which other metal can be used to reduce alkyl halides?
rationales: Al is not the metal specified for this reduction in the chapter method.
Magnesium can be used to reduce alkyl halides.
Nickel is commonly used as a catalyst in other reactions, but is not the answer here.
Cobalt is not the metal specified for this reduction.

mcqs.stem: If naphtha undergoes a combustion reaction what products do you expect to form?
rationales: Alkanes are not the products of complete combustion.
Alkenes are not the products of complete combustion.
Complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water.
A mixture of alkanes and alkenes is not the expected combustion product.

options: Because zinc acts as a reducing agent.
Because atomic hydrogen is produced with Zn / HCl which acts as a reducing agent.
Because molecular hydrogen is produced with Zn / HCl which acts as a reducing agent.
Because chloride ions are produced with Zn / HCl which act as a reducing agent.
mcqs.stem: Why does a mixture of zinc and hydrochloric acid acts as a reducing agent?
rationales: The textbook explanation is the reducing action of newly produced atomic hydrogen, not zinc acting alone.
Atomic hydrogen produced by Zn/HCl acts as a reducing agent.
The textbook explanation identifies atomic rather than molecular hydrogen as the reducing agent.
Chloride ions are not the reducing agent in this reaction.

mcqs.stem: Which alkane will evolve the most amount of heat when it is burnt with oxygen?
rationales: Ethane has fewer carbon atoms than the butanes and releases less heat per mole on combustion.
Propane has fewer carbon atoms than the butanes and releases less heat per mole on combustion.
n-Butane is the expected choice; it has the greatest heat of combustion among these choices.
iso-Butane is a branched isomer and releases slightly less heat than n-butane on combustion.

mcqs.stem: Which reaction is not given by alkanes?
rationales: Alkanes undergo substitution reactions, such as halogenation.
Alkanes undergo combustion reactions.
Addition is characteristic of unsaturated hydrocarbons; alkanes do not normally undergo addition.
Alkanes can undergo cracking.

mcqs.stem: Which hydrocarbon is responsible for explosions in coal mines?
rationales: Butane is not the gas responsible for the familiar coal-mine explosions.
Pentane is not the gas responsible for the familiar coal-mine explosions.
Methane can mix with air and form an explosive mixture in coal mines.
Ethene is not the gas identified as responsible for coal-mine explosions.

mcqs.stem: Which product will be formed when ethyl bromide (CH₃ CH₂ Br) is treated with Zn/HCl
rationales: CH₄ has one carbon atom, whereas the reaction retains the two-carbon chain.
Reduction replaces bromine with hydrogen, forming ethane, CH₃—CH₃.
This product has four carbon atoms, which are not present in ethyl bromide.
This product has three carbon atoms, which are not present in ethyl bromide.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following is not a process of halogenation of alkanes?
rationales: Cracking breaks larger hydrocarbons into smaller ones; it is not halogenation.
Chlorination is halogenation with chlorine.
Bromination is halogenation with bromine.
Iodination is halogenation with iodine.

mcqs.stem: How many moles of oxygen will be required to completely burn propane?
rationales: Four moles of oxygen do not balance the combustion equation.
Five moles of oxygen balance C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O.
Three moles of oxygen are insufficient to balance complete combustion.
Six moles of oxygen are more than required by the balanced equation.

written.text: Differentiate between an organic and an inorganic compound.
written.finalAnswer: Organic compounds are generally carbon compounds, usually containing hydrogen; inorganic compounds are generally compounds not classified as organic.

rubric.why: The distinction must identify the usual composition of organic compounds.
rubric.description: State the general composition of organic compounds.
rubric.how: Mention carbon, usually with hydrogen.

rubric.why: The answer must contrast organic compounds with inorganic compounds.
rubric.how: State that inorganic compounds are generally not classified as organic.

modelAnswer: Organic compounds are generally carbon compounds, usually containing hydrogen.
Inorganic compounds are generally compounds not classified as organic.

written.text: Why are organic compounds found in large numbers?
written.finalAnswer: Carbon forms stable covalent bonds with itself and other elements, allowing chains, branches and rings and many different compounds.

rubric.why: Carbon's ability to bond to itself is central to the large number of organic compounds.
rubric.how: State that carbon atoms form stable bonds with one another.

rubric.why: Different structures explain how many distinct compounds can form.
rubric.how: Mention chains, branches or rings and bonding with other elements.

modelAnswer: Carbon forms stable covalent bonds with itself and with other elements.
It can form chains, branches and rings, producing a very large number of compounds.

written.text: Name the products which are obtained when natural gas is oxidized under controlled conditions.
written.finalAnswer: Methanol and formaldehyde.

rubric.why: Methanol is one product named for controlled oxidation of natural gas.
rubric.how: Write methanol.

rubric.why: Formaldehyde is the other product expected.
rubric.how: Write formaldehyde (methanal).

modelAnswer: Methanol and formaldehyde are obtained when natural gas is oxidized under controlled conditions.

written.text: How naphtha fraction is decomposed to give lower hydrocarbons?
written.finalAnswer: By cracking: naphtha is heated, often in the presence of a catalyst, and decomposes into lower hydrocarbons.

rubric.why: The process name is essential.
rubric.how: State that naphtha undergoes cracking.

rubric.why: Cracking involves heating the larger hydrocarbons to form smaller ones.
rubric.how: Explain that heating decomposes naphtha into lower hydrocarbons.

modelAnswer: Naphtha is decomposed by cracking.
It is heated, often in the presence of a catalyst, to give lower hydrocarbons.

written.text: Write down the molecular formula, structural formula and the condensed structural formula for iso-butane.
written.finalAnswer: Molecular formula: C₄H₁₀; structural formula: CH₃—CH(CH₃)—CH₃; condensed structural formula: (CH₃)₃CH.

rubric.why: The molecular formula gives the total atoms in the molecule.
rubric.how: Write C₄H₁₀.

rubric.why: The structural representation must show the branched carbon skeleton of iso-butane.
rubric.description: Give a structural or condensed representation.
rubric.how: Show a three-carbon chain with a methyl branch on the middle carbon.

rubric.why: The condensed formula must express the branched arrangement compactly.
rubric.how: Write (CH₃)₃CH or an equivalent condensed form.

modelAnswer: Molecular formula: C₄H₁₀
Structural formula: CH₃—CH(CH₃)—CH₃
Condensed structural formula: (CH₃)₃CH

written.text: How are organic compounds useful for us?
written.finalAnswer: Organic compounds are used as food, fuels, medicines, clothing materials and many other useful products.

rubric.why: Examples show the everyday uses of organic compounds.
rubric.how: Name at least two uses.

rubric.why: The answer should make clear their broad importance in everyday life.
rubric.how: State that organic compounds are important in daily life or industry.

modelAnswer: Organic compounds are useful as food, fuels, medicines and clothing materials.
They are also used in many other products of daily life and industry.

written.text: Write down the names of five such organic compounds which exist naturally?
written.finalAnswer: Examples include glucose, starch, cellulose, proteins and fats.

rubric.why: The response needs natural examples of organic compounds.
rubric.how: Give at least three valid examples.

rubric.why: The question asks for five examples.
rubric.how: Name five valid naturally occurring organic compounds.

modelAnswer: Glucose, starch, cellulose, proteins and fats are organic compounds which exist naturally.

written.text: Give IUPAC name to the following compound. [FIGURE: Structural formula CH₃—CH—CH₂—CH₃, with CH₃ attached below the CH group.]
written.finalAnswer: 2-methylbutane

rubric.why: The longest continuous chain contains four carbon atoms.
rubric.description: Select and name the parent chain.
rubric.how: Identify the parent as butane.

rubric.why: The substituent position and name complete the IUPAC name.
rubric.how: Number from the nearer end and name the methyl group at carbon 2.

modelAnswer: The longest continuous chain has four carbon atoms, so the parent name is butane.
Numbering from the nearer end places the methyl group on carbon 2.
IUPAC name: 2-methylbutane.

written.text: How do the melting and boiling points of alkanes change when we move from lower members to higher members?
written.finalAnswer: The melting and boiling points generally increase as the molecular size and molecular mass of alkanes increase.

rubric.why: The direction of the trend must be correct.
rubric.how: Say that melting and boiling points rise from lower to higher members.

rubric.why: A reason links the trend to the growing molecules and stronger attractions.
rubric.how: Relate the trend to larger molecules and greater intermolecular attraction.

modelAnswer: The melting and boiling points of alkanes generally increase from lower members to higher members.
This is because molecular size and molecular mass increase.

written.text: Why do alkanes show little reactivity towards the other reagents?
written.finalAnswer: Alkanes contain strong C—C and C—H single covalent bonds and have no reactive functional group, so they are relatively unreactive.

rubric.why: Strong bonds are difficult for reagents to break.
rubric.how: Mention the strong C—C and C—H bonds.

rubric.why: The absence of a reactive functional group explains their low reactivity.
rubric.how: State that alkanes lack a reactive functional group.

modelAnswer: Alkanes contain strong C—C and C—H single covalent bonds.
They have no reactive functional group, so they show little reactivity towards other reagents.

written.text: Why does a mixture of natural gas and air explode?
written.finalAnswer: Natural gas mixes with oxygen in air; when ignited, it burns very rapidly and releases a large amount of heat, causing an explosion.

rubric.why: An explosive mixture requires natural gas mixed with oxygen from air.
rubric.how: State that natural gas mixes with oxygen in air.

rubric.why: Rapid combustion and heat release explain the explosion.
rubric.how: Say that ignition causes rapid combustion and a sudden release of heat.

modelAnswer: Natural gas forms a mixture with oxygen present in air.
When ignited, it burns rapidly and releases a large amount of heat, causing an explosion.

written.text: How do you compare the melting and boiling points of inorganic and organic compounds?
written.finalAnswer: Organic compounds generally have lower melting and boiling points than inorganic compounds because many organic compounds are molecular substances with weaker intermolecular forces.

rubric.why: The comparison must give the usual relative melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: State that organic compounds generally have lower melting and boiling points.

rubric.why: The explanation links the difference to the nature of bonding and attractions.
rubric.how: Refer to weaker forces between organic molecules compared with strong attractions in many inorganic compounds.

modelAnswer: Organic compounds generally have lower melting and boiling points than inorganic compounds.
Many organic compounds are molecular substances with weaker intermolecular forces.

written.text: Reactions of alkanes with chlorine takes place in the presence of sunlight. What is the role of sunlight in the reaction?
written.finalAnswer: Sunlight supplies energy to break the Cl—Cl bond homolytically, producing chlorine free radicals that initiate the substitution reaction.

rubric.why: Sunlight starts the reaction by supplying energy to break the chlorine bond.
rubric.how: Explain that sunlight provides energy to break the Cl—Cl bond.

rubric.why: The resulting radicals initiate the substitution reaction.
rubric.how: Mention formation of chlorine radicals and initiation of substitution.

modelAnswer: Sunlight supplies energy to break the Cl—Cl bond homolytically.
Chlorine free radicals are formed and initiate the substitution reaction.

written.text: How do you compare the boiling point of n – butane with that of iso – butane?
written.finalAnswer: n-Butane has a higher boiling point than iso-butane because its straight-chain molecules have a larger area of contact and stronger intermolecular attractions.

rubric.why: The comparison must correctly identify which isomer boils at the higher temperature.
rubric.how: State that n-butane has the higher boiling point.

rubric.why: The structural reason explains the difference between the isomers.
rubric.how: Relate the straight-chain shape to greater contact and stronger attractions.

modelAnswer: n-Butane has a higher boiling point than iso-butane.
The straight-chain molecules have a larger area of contact and stronger intermolecular attractions.

written.text: Why are organic compounds not generally soluble in water?
written.finalAnswer: Most organic compounds are non-polar, whereas water is polar; therefore, they do not generally dissolve in water.

rubric.why: The polarity of organic compounds is part of the explanation.
rubric.description: Identify the nature of organic compounds.
rubric.how: State that most organic compounds are non-polar.

rubric.why: The contrast with polar water explains their poor solubility.
rubric.how: Explain that non-polar compounds do not generally dissolve in polar water.

modelAnswer: Most organic compounds are non-polar, whereas water is polar.
Therefore, organic compounds are not generally soluble in water.

written.text: Describe the importance of organic compounds in daily life.
written.finalAnswer: Organic compounds are important in food, fuels, medicines, clothing, plastics and many other materials used in everyday life.

rubric.why: Food substances are a major everyday use and occurrence of organic compounds.
rubric.how: Give food nutrients or natural organic substances as examples.

rubric.why: Organic compounds are important energy sources.
rubric.how: Give fuels such as natural gas or petrol.

rubric.why: Medicines are an important practical use.
rubric.how: State that many medicines are organic compounds.

rubric.why: Further examples show their broad use in everyday materials.
rubric.how: Mention clothing fibres, plastics, dyes or other useful products.

modelAnswer: Organic compounds are important constituents of food, including carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
Many organic compounds are used as fuels, such as natural gas and petrol.
Many medicines and drugs are organic compounds.
Organic compounds are also used to make clothing fibres, plastics, dyes and many other products used in daily life.

written.text: Why is carbon so important as an element that the whole branch of chemistry is based on it?
written.finalAnswer: Carbon forms four stable covalent bonds, bonds strongly with itself and many other elements, and forms chains, branches and rings; this creates a vast number of compounds.

rubric.why: Carbon's valency allows it to form many stable compounds.
rubric.how: Mention four covalent bonds or tetravalency.

rubric.why: Carbon-to-carbon bonding allows large structures.
rubric.how: State that carbon bonds strongly with itself.

rubric.why: Different structures increase the variety of compounds.
rubric.how: Name chains, branches or rings.

rubric.why: The combination of bonding properties explains why a whole branch studies carbon compounds.
rubric.how: State that these properties produce a vast number of compounds.

modelAnswer: Carbon is tetravalent and forms four stable covalent bonds.
Carbon atoms bond strongly with one another and with atoms of many other elements.
Carbon can form straight chains, branched chains and rings.
These properties produce a vast number of carbon compounds, which are studied in organic chemistry.

written.text: A carbon–carbon single bond (C – C) in alkanes does not behave as a functional group but a carbon carbon double bond (C = C) in alkenes does. Explain.
written.finalAnswer: The C—C single bond in alkanes is strong and relatively unreactive, so it does not determine characteristic reactions. The C=C double bond in alkenes contains a reactive π bond, which readily undergoes addition reactions and acts as a functional group.

rubric.why: The answer must distinguish the alkane single bond.
rubric.how: State that the alkane C—C single bond is strong and relatively unreactive.

rubric.why: This explains why the single bond does not determine a characteristic reaction pattern.
rubric.how: Say it does not act as a functional group.

rubric.why: The contrasting alkene bond must be identified.
rubric.how: Mention the C=C double bond and its reactive π bond.

rubric.why: Characteristic reactions explain why the double bond acts as a functional group.
rubric.how: State that it readily undergoes addition reactions.

modelAnswer: The C—C single bond in alkanes is strong and relatively unreactive.
It does not determine characteristic reactions and does not behave as a functional group.
The C=C double bond in alkenes contains a reactive π bond.
It readily undergoes addition reactions, so it behaves as a functional group.

written.text: Explain IUPAC system of nomenclature for alkanes.
written.finalAnswer: Choose the longest continuous carbon chain as the parent alkane; number it from the end nearest a branch; name and number each alkyl substituent; use prefixes for repeated substituents and arrange different substituent names alphabetically.

rubric.why: Selecting the parent chain determines the base name.
rubric.how: State that the longest continuous chain is selected.

rubric.why: Correct numbering gives the substituent the lowest possible position.
rubric.how: Number from the end nearer the first branch.

rubric.why: Substituents must be named and their positions shown.
rubric.how: Give the substituent name with its position number.

rubric.why: Standard ordering and punctuation complete the systematic name.
rubric.how: Mention alphabetical order for different substituents and prefixes for repeated groups.

modelAnswer: Select the longest continuous carbon chain and use the corresponding alkane name as the parent name.
Number the chain from the end nearer the first branch so the substituents receive the lowest possible numbers.
Name each alkyl substituent and write its position number before its name.
Use di-, tri- and other prefixes for repeated substituents; arrange different substituent names alphabetically.

written.text: How combustion reaction of alkanes is useful for us?
written.finalAnswer: Combustion of alkanes releases heat energy, so alkanes are useful as fuels for cooking, heating and transport.

rubric.why: Identify the process that releases useful energy.
rubric.how: State that alkanes burn in oxygen.

rubric.why: Heat release is the direct useful result of combustion.
rubric.how: Mention release of heat or energy.

rubric.why: These are practical uses of the released energy.
rubric.how: Name cooking or heating.

rubric.why: Fuel use extends the importance of combustion to transport.
rubric.how: Mention use as fuel in transport or engines.

modelAnswer: Alkanes burn in oxygen in a combustion reaction and release heat energy.
This heat is used for cooking and heating.
Alkanes are also used as fuels for transport and engines.

written.text: When natural gas valve is kept open in the kitchen, the gas spreads through the whole kitchen. This may cause an explosion. What is the reason of this explosion and how can you avoid it?
written.finalAnswer: Natural gas mixes with air and may form an explosive mixture; a spark or flame can ignite it and cause rapid combustion. Close the valve, avoid flames and electrical switches, ventilate the room, and have the leak checked safely.

rubric.why: The hazard begins when leaking gas mixes with air.
rubric.how: State that natural gas mixes with oxygen in air.

rubric.why: An ignition source causes rapid combustion and the explosion risk.
rubric.how: Mention ignition by a spark or flame.

rubric.why: Stopping the gas leak is the first safety action.
rubric.how: Close the gas valve if it is safe to do so.

rubric.why: Safe ventilation and avoiding ignition sources reduce danger.
rubric.how: Avoid flames and switches, ventilate, and seek safe leak assistance.

modelAnswer: Leaking natural gas mixes with oxygen in the kitchen air and can form an explosive mixture.
A spark or flame can ignite the mixture, causing rapid combustion and an explosion.
Close the gas valve if it is safe; do not light flames or operate electrical switches.
Ventilate the kitchen and have the leak checked safely.

written.text: “Neem” is a common tree grown throughout our country. Comment on the medicinal benefits of this tree.
written.finalAnswer: Neem has traditionally been used for its antiseptic and antimicrobial properties, including in skin care and oral hygiene; it should not be used as a medicine without appropriate medical advice.

rubric.why: The response must address neem's medicinal use.
rubric.how: State that neem is traditionally used medicinally.

rubric.why: These are relevant medicinal properties commonly associated with neem.
rubric.how: Name antiseptic or antimicrobial properties.

rubric.why: Examples make the claimed uses concrete.
rubric.how: Mention traditional skin or oral-hygiene uses.

rubric.why: A safe answer avoids presenting traditional use as a substitute for medical care.
rubric.how: Advise appropriate professional guidance before medicinal use.

modelAnswer: Neem has traditionally been used for its antiseptic and antimicrobial properties.
Neem preparations are used traditionally in skin care and oral hygiene.
Such traditional uses do not replace medical treatment.
Neem should not be used as a medicine without appropriate medical advice.

written.text: Name a few popular medicines which are, in fact, organic compounds?
written.finalAnswer: Examples include aspirin, paracetamol and penicillin.

rubric.why: Aspirin is a valid example of an organic medicine.
rubric.how: Write aspirin.

rubric.why: Paracetamol is a valid example of an organic medicine.
rubric.how: Write paracetamol.

rubric.why: Penicillin is a valid example of an organic medicine.
rubric.how: Write penicillin.

rubric.why: The answer should make clear these named substances are medicines and organic compounds.
rubric.how: Identify the examples as organic medicines.

modelAnswer: Aspirin, paracetamol and penicillin are popular medicines which are organic compounds.

examTips: Short questions commonly ask for definitions, examples, formulas, names and one-sentence explanations; give the key term directly.
Constructed-response questions often ask why or compare; state the fact and then give the chemical reason.
For IUPAC naming, show the longest chain, numbering and substituent position before writing the final name.
For combustion questions, write and balance the equation carefully; show the oxygen coefficient clearly.
Long descriptive questions are marked for separate relevant points, so use clear point-by-point statements.
In safety questions, explain both the chemical hazard and practical steps to prevent ignition.

Compare the contact area of straight-chain and branched molecules.

steps.why: The formula of propane shows 3 carbon atoms and 8 hydrogen atoms.
Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon forms carbon dioxide and water.
Balance carbon first, then hydrogen, to find the product coefficients.
The products contain 10 oxygen atoms, so 5 O₂ molecules are required.
The coefficients give the required mole ratio for complete combustion.
steps.text: Answer: 1 mol C₃H₈ requires 5 mol O₂.

explain.title: Carbon compounds are numerous
explain.body: Carbon forms strong covalent bonds with itself and other elements. It can make chains, branches and rings, so a very large number of organic compounds exist.

explain.title: Alkanes and their reactions
explain.body: Alkanes have carbon–carbon single bonds. They are relatively unreactive, but undergo combustion, substitution (such as halogenation) and cracking. They do not normally undergo addition.

explain.title: Combustion and safety
explain.body: Complete combustion of hydrocarbons produces carbon dioxide and water and releases heat. Natural gas mixed with air can be explosive if ignited, so leaks need immediate safe attention.

explain.title: Names and properties
explain.body: For an alkane name, select the longest chain, number it from the nearer end to a branch, and name the substituents. As alkane size generally increases, melting and boiling points rise; among isomers, branching usually lowers boiling point.

mistakes: Do not say that addition is a normal reaction of alkanes; addition is characteristic of unsaturated hydrocarbons.
Do not confuse cracking, which breaks hydrocarbons into smaller molecules, with halogenation.
When naming a branched alkane, number from the end nearest the substituent and include its position number.
For complete combustion of propane, do not leave the oxygen coefficient unbalanced: it is 5O₂.
Do not claim organic compounds are all soluble in water; most are generally non-polar and do not dissolve well in polar water.
When comparing n-butane and iso-butane, remember that n-butane has the higher boiling point.
